analysis.one_liner: Bans online ads targeted to a person's personal data, allowing only ads based on the content being viewed.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in September 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit advertisers and the companies that deliver online ads from targeting ads at individuals based on their personal information, including browsing history, contact details, and device identifiers. It would allow ads based on the content a person is currently viewing or searching for, and ads aimed at broad geographic areas like a state or metro area, but not profiling. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals could all enforce the ban, and pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers would be unenforceable for claims under the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet or a connected device: their data — browsing history, contact information, device identifiers — could no longer be used to select which ads they see, limiting the profiling that drives surveillance advertising. The private right of action with statutory damages and access to court (no forced arbitration) gives ordinary users a way to sue violators directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users whose data feeds ad targeting

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars advertisers and advertising facilitators from targeting ads using personal information, including contact details, unique device identifiers, browsing history, and data inferred from collected data.

It preserves contextual advertising — ads shown based on the page or content a person is viewing or searching for — while barring that data from being reused for further targeting, and it permits ads aimed at broad recognized places such as a state, county, congressional district, or designated market area.

Enforcement is layered: the FTC treats violations as unfair or deceptive practices and gains authority over common carriers and nonprofits, state attorneys general can sue on behalf of residents, and individuals can sue for $100–$1,000 per negligent violation or $500–$5,000 per willful violation, with attorney's fees available.

Pre-dispute arbitration agreements and pre-dispute class-action waivers are invalid for claims under the Act, with a court rather than an arbitrator deciding that question, so users can bring claims in court.

analysis.who_pays: Digital advertising platforms and ad-tech intermediaries lose the core of the targeted-advertising business model, which depends on collecting and processing personal information to select who sees each ad. Data brokers lose demand for the personal information they sell for targeting. Advertisers, including small businesses that use cheap precise targeting, would pay to reach customers through blunter contextual and geographic channels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ad platforms, data brokers, and targeted advertisers

drawbacks.text: Advertisers — including small businesses that rely on inexpensive, precise online targeting to reach customers — would lose their most efficient marketing channel and could face higher costs reaching buyers.

The ban is narrower than its title suggests: contextual advertising and place-based targeting (state, county, metro area, congressional district) remain lawful, so a considerable amount of audience selection survives.

A private right of action with per-violation statutory damages ($100–$5,000), no arbitration, and no class-action waiver could generate substantial litigation against companies over advertising practices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and broad: it would end the practice of selecting ads for individuals based on their personal data, curbing pervasive profiling of internet users and giving them enforceable court rights rather than arbitration. The costs fall mostly on the ad-tech industry and data brokers, whose business models depend on the prohibited practice, though advertisers that depended on cheap precise targeting — especially small ones — would face higher marketing costs, and free online services funded by targeted ads might shift toward subscriptions, less relevant ads, or reduced services. On balance, the bill asks the industry with the most at stake to absorb a change in how it sells access to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittee, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo, joined by Rep. Jan Schakowsky, introduced the bill on September 18, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
Four days later, on September 22, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce.
The action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill's only cosponsor was a House Democrat, and no Senate companion action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Digital ad platforms and data brokers kept their targeted-advertising business model intact, since the prohibition was never acted on. Internet users gained nothing because the profiling ban never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Digital ad platforms and data brokers

for.name: Rep. Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Banning Surveillance Advertising Act of 2023 in the House.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce
against.role: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee where the bill was parked
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 22, 2023 and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-controlled in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its initial referral and never advanced it to the full committee or the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were House Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.industry: Digital advertising platforms and ad-tech intermediaries
industries.note: These companies are paid to choose which individual or device sees each ad, and the bill makes that selection based on personal information illegal, removing the profiling that underpins their revenue. Their interest in defeating the bill runs directly against the privacy interest of internet users.

Brokers sell personal data used for targeting, and the bill bans supplying contact information, device identifiers, and other personal data for that purpose, cutting off a major market. Their loss would come from users no longer being profiled.

industries.industry: Advertisers, including small businesses and e-commerce brands
industries.note: They lose cheap, precise individual targeting and would rely on contextual and place-based ads instead, which could raise the cost of reaching customers. The same change stops their ads from being delivered through surveillance of the people they are trying to reach.
